text.en: When a magnesium ribbon is held in a flame it burns with a dazzling white light and leaves a white powder. A new substance forms, so a chemical reaction has happened. We record it using a chemical equation.

A chemical reaction changes substances into new ones. Signs include a change in state, colour, temperature, or the evolution of a gas.
We write a word equation first: magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide. Reactants are on the left and products on the right.
A skeletal equation uses formulae: Mg + O2 gives MgO. It is not balanced because oxygen atoms are 2 on the left and 1 on the right.
The law of conservation of mass says that mass is neither created nor destroyed, so the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides.
We balance by changing coefficients, never the formulae: 2Mg + O2 gives 2MgO.
Step by step: count atoms, balance the element that appears in one reactant and one product first, then hydrogen and oxygen last.
We add state symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous. A reaction condition such as heat is written over the arrow.
For iron reacting with steam: 3Fe + 4H2O gives Fe3O4 + 4H2 is the balanced equation.

Left has 2 O atoms, right has 1, so put 2 before H2O: H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
Now hydrogen is 2 on the left and 4 on the right, so put 2 before H2.
2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, with 4 H and 2 O on each side.

prompt.en: Why must a chemical equation be balanced and how is it done?

commonMisconceptions.en: Changing the subscripts in a formula

points.en: A chemical equation shows reactants and products.
Balance by changing coefficients so atoms are equal on both sides.
